title: Photo tips: framing and composition
h1: Photo tips: framing and composition to sell
metaTitle: Product Photography: 6 Framing Rules for Images That Convert
description: Master the art of product photography with our 6 essential framing and composition tips. Discover how to transform your e-commerce images into real sales tools, regardless of your equipment. Practical guide for photographers and e-retailers.
author: PackshotCreator
content:
Before even thinking about framing or composing a photo, an essential question must be asked: Why are you taking this photo? In other words, what do you want to show, tell, or make people feel?
‍This intention will guide your technical and creative choices throughout the shoot. This is even more true in the context of product photography, where each image should grab attention, build trust... and sell.

1. Intent over technique: define your visual message

Here are a few simple questions to guide your approach:

  • What is the main subject?
  • What context should be included or excluded?
  • Do you need to highlight details or rather show the wider scene?
  • How should the viewer feel when looking at this image?

‍

‍

Concrete examples:

  • A luxury piece of jewelry with a meticulous finish? → Fill the frame to show the material.
  • A pair of shoes in a lifestyle environment? → Leave space around it to tell a story.
  • A bag being worn? → Think about the relationship between the subject, the wearer and the viewer's gaze.

2. Fill or aerate: find the right balance for your product

One of the first compositional choices is to decide on the relationship between the subject and the space that surrounds it. Here are a few useful guidelines:

Fill the frame if:

  • The subject is rare, complex, or rich in detail
  • You want to create a strong relationship with the observer
  • You want to maximize visual impact in a small space (e.g. e-commerce thumbnails)

Do not fill the frame if:

  • The environment or the staging gives meaning to the image
  • You want to suggest a world or an atmosphere
  • The movement or the gaze of the subject needs space to express itself

3. The composition at the service of your product

➤ Place the subject off-center. It's a basic rule of photography: avoid placing the subject in the center of the image. A subject placed too centrally often gives a static, frozen impression.

➤ Leave space around the subject. Avoid placing the object right against the edges. Give it some visual breathing room, especially if it is in motion or “looking” in one direction.

➤ Do not follow the central axes. Unless you deliberately choose otherwise for aesthetic reasons, it is better not to align important elements on the central vertical or horizontal axes of the frame.

4. The rule of thirds: position your products strategically

The rule of thirds is a classic method of visual composition, inherited from painting. It consists of dividing your image into nine equal parts using two horizontal and two vertical lines.
The intersection points of these lines are called “power points”. They are natural locations to position the subject or key elements.

‍

‍

Examples:

  • In landscape photography, place the horizon on the lower or upper third, never in the center.
  • For a packshot of glasses, position the lenses on one of the thirds lines, and not right in the center of the image.
  • For a hand-held product, ensure that the model's gaze falls on one of the power points.

5. Create movement: bring your packshots to life

Even in a still packshot, it is important to leave space in front of the gaze or movement of the subject. This creates a sense of movement.
Whether the movement is real (e.g. a step, a rotation) or suggested (a gaze, an orientation), it needs room to express itself in the image.

6. From the pro studio to the internal solution: accessible quality

All of these rules also apply to packshot photography, even when automated. Whether you are using an e-commerce photo studio such as the Alphashot Pro G2 or a conventional shooting solution, composition remains a matter of choice.
For example, find out how an online store can photograph its shoes with an in-house photo studio to guarantee uniform, consistent and striking results.

Conclusion: Rules... or guidelines?

The principles we have just covered are not fixed laws, but guidelines to help you structure your shots. Photography is also a matter of instinct. If another composition seems more aesthetically pleasing, more faithful to your visual message, make that choice.
What matters is to stay consistent with your intention, with the perception that you want to create, and with the intended use of the image.
Before thinking about framing or composing your photos, ask yourself why you want to take this photo, what you want to show, tell, or make people feel with it.

faqs.question: What is the ideal distance to photograph a product?
faqs.answer: The ideal distance depends on the product and your objective. For small items that require detail (jewelry, watches), get closer using a macro lens. For larger products (clothing, furniture), step back far enough to capture the whole product while maintaining good definition. The main thing is to maintain sharpness on important elements and avoid distortions.

faqs.question: Should you always use a white background for product photography?
faqs.answer: No, although the white background is standard for e-commerce sites, other options can enhance your product. The background must be chosen according to your target and the desired atmosphere. A contextual background can tell a story, while a plain colored background can create a strong visual identity. The important thing is consistency across your catalog.

faqs.question: How do you avoid unwanted reflections on shiny products?
faqs.answer: For shiny products (jewelry, glasses, metal objects), use diffused lighting with softboxes or umbrellas. Place your lighting at 45° to the product and use reflectors to control the shadows. For highly reflective surfaces, a diffusion tent may be required. Feel free to use polarizers to eliminate specular reflections.

faqs.question: What camera settings should I use for product photography?
faqs.answer: Choose a low ISO sensitivity (100-200) to maximize image quality. Use a medium aperture (f/8 to f/11) to get a good depth of field. Shutter speed is less critical if you're using a tripod. In manual mode, adjust your white balance according to your lighting for accurate colors. Shoot in RAW for more post-processing flexibility.

faqs.question: What is the difference between packshot photography and lifestyle product photography?
faqs.answer: Packshot photography focuses on the isolated product, usually on a neutral background, to clearly show its characteristics and details. It is essential for e-commerce product pages. Lifestyle photography, on the other hand, shows the product in use, in a real context or environment. It allows you to tell a story, to evoke a lifestyle and to show the function of the product. A comprehensive visual strategy often combines these two approaches: packshots to inform, lifestyle to inspire and create an emotional connection.
